Reference Link: https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/doc/Key_to_Budget_Document_2026.pdf https://prsindia.org/files/budget/budget_parliament/2026/Union_Budget_Anal ysis-2026-27.pdf https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2221455&reg=3&lang=1 !!! Quiz on Union Budget 2026-27 will soon be covered daily on our CareersCloud App for your effective revision. Stay tuned!!!! Union Budget 2026-2027 What is the Budget? The budget is referred to as an Annual Financial Statement (AFS) of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government in a Financial Year (which begins on 1st April of the current year and ends on 31st March of the following year) under Article 112 of the Constitution of India. Prepared by: It is prepared by the Department of Economic Affairs in the Ministry of Finance (MoF). Union Budget 2026-27 Budget Announcement: On February 1,2026 the Budget session was held in Parliament under the chairmanship of Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla, in which the Union Finance Minister (FM) Nirmala Sitharaman presented the Union Budget of India for 2026-2027. • This is said to be India’s 6th paperless budget and 1st Budget prepared in Kartavya Bhawan (Common Central Secretariat). • It was the 12th budget of the Narendra Modi-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA). It was also the 7th Budget presentation of Nirmala Sitharaman since 2019. Finance Minister Speech Speech Duration: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman delivered her budget speech for the 2026-27 Union Budget lasting 85 minutes (mins). • Longest Full Budget (2020) - 162 Minutes (2 hours, 42 mins) • Shortest Full Budget (2025) - 74 Minutes (1 hour, 14 mins) • Shortest Interim (2024) - 57 Minutes Significance It became the first Union Budget to be delivered on a Sunday in independent India. This will be Ms. Sitharaman’s ninth consecutive Budget, making her the first woman finance minister to achieve this milestone • This will take Ms. Sitharaman closer to the record of 10 Budgets that were presented by former Prime Minister Morarji Desai over different time periods. Desai presented a total of 6 budgets during his tenure as Finance Minister in 1959-1964, and 4 Budgets between 1967-1969.

# Page 5^page=5
Report Errors in the PDF - support@affairscloud.com Copyright 2014-2026 @ AffairsCloud.com 5 Union Budget 2026-27 • Former Finance Ministers P Chidambaram and Pranab Mukherjee had presented nine and eight Budgets, respectively, under different Prime Ministers. Budget Focus Focus: The FM described this year’s budget as “Yuva Shakti–driven Budget”, Converting India’s demographic dividend into productive capacity through skilling, employment, and enterprise creation. Fiscal Position Receipts: The receipts (other than borrowings) in 2026-27 are estimated to be Rs 36,51,547 crore (Cr), about 7.2% higher than the Revised Estimate (RE) of 2025-26. Expenditure: The government is estimated to spend Rs 53,47,315 Cr in 2026-27, 7.7% higher than the RE of 2025-26. Kartavyas The Union Budget is inspired by 3 kartavyas: • 1st Kartavya: To accelerate and sustain economic growth, by enhancing productivity and competitiveness, and building resilience to volatile global dynamics. • 2nd Kartavya: To fulfil aspirations of people and build their capacity, making them strong partners in India’s path to prosperity. • 3rd Kartavya: To ensure that every family, community, region and sector has access to resources, amenities and opportunities for meaningful participation. Highlights of India’s Fiscal Position Fiscal Deficit (FD): The Budget Estimate (BE) for 2026-27 sets the FD at 4.3% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), lower than the RE of 4.4% of GDP in 2025-26. • Revenue deficit (RD) in 2026-27 is targeted at 1.5% of GDP. This is similar to the RE of 1.5% in 2025-26. • Primary deficit (PD) is fiscal deficit less interest payments. It is estimated to be 0.7% of GDP in 2026-27. Note: FD is the difference between total expenditure and total receipts (excluding Debt Capital Receipts). RD is the excess of revenue expenditure over revenue receipts. GDP: GDP: The government has estimated a nominal GDP growth rate of 10% in 2026-27 (i.e., real growth plus inflation) Nominal GDP: The government has estimated a nominal GDP growth rate of 10% in 2026-27 (i.e., real growth plus inflation). Debt: The central government aims to reduce its outstanding liabilities to around 50% of GDP by March 2031. • In 2026-27, outstanding liabilities are estimated to be 55.6% of the GDP. The interest payment is estimated to be 40% of revenue receipts in 2026-27. Taxation: The government has not made any modification to the direct income tax rates and slabs in this budget.

Of this, the government has estimated to raise Rs 10,19,020 Cr from CGST (Central GST). • Corporation Tax: In 2026-27, the collection from taxes on companies is expected to increase by 11% over the RE for 2025-26. • Income Tax: Income tax collection is expected to increase by 11.7% in 2026-27. • Non-Tax revenue: Non-tax revenue is estimated at Rs 6,66,228 Cr in 2026-27, roughly same as the RE for 2025-26. o 59% of the non-tax revenue in 2026-27 is estimated to come from dividend and profits. Total Receipts: Government receipts (excluding borrowings) are estimated at Rs 36,51,547 Cr, 7.2% higher than the RE of 2025-26. • The gap between these receipts and the expenditure will be bridged by borrowings of Rs 16,95,767 Cr. Transfer to States: The central government will transfer Rs 26,20,769 Cr to states in 2026-27, an increase of 12.2% over the RE of 2025-26.

Report Errors in the PDF - support@affairscloud.com Copyright 2014-2026 @ AffairsCloud.com 7 Union Budget 2026-27 • Transfer to states includes tax devolution of Rs 15,26,255 Cr and grants and loans worth Rs 10,94,514 Cr. Miscellaneous Capital Receipts: Centre has set an ambitious disinvestment target of Rs 80,000 crore under miscellaneous capital receipts for 2026-27 which includes sale of shares in Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) as well as asset monetisations. • In 2025-26, the government had budgeted Rs 47,000 crore from miscellaneous capital receipts, but collections lagged through the year, prompting a cut in the revised estimate to Rs 34,169 crore. Actual receipts in 2024-25 were even lower at Rs 20,214 crore Ministry Allocation 2026-27 In 2026-27, the top 13 ministries in terms of allocations account for 54% of the estimated total expenditure. • The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has the highest allocation in 2026-27, at Rs 7,84,678 Cr, accounting for 15% of the total budgeted expenditure of the central government. • Other ministries with high allocations include: Road Transport and Highways (6% of total expenditure), Railways (5%), and Home Affairs (5%). Ministry of Jal Shakti (MoJS): Allocation is estimated to increase by Rs 53,371 crore in 2026-27, over the revised estimates of 2025-26. Revised estimate for 2025-26 was Rs 41,437 crore as compared to budgeted Rs 99,503 crore. Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoH&UA): Allocation towards this ministry is estimated to increase by Rs 28,318 Cr (49.5%) to Rs 85,522 Cr in 2026-27. • This is primarily due to increased allocation towards Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Urban (PMAY-U), with an underspending of Rs 22,332 Cr between budgeted and revised estimates of 2025-26. Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilisers: Allocation towards Chemicals and Fertilisers is estimated to decrease by Rs 14,125 Cr (7.4%) to Rs 1,77,061 Cr in 2025-26. This is primarily due to decrease in fertiliser subsidy. First Kartavya – Accelerate and Sustain economic growth Scaling up manufacturing in 7 strategic and frontier sectors: i. Biopharma SHAKTI (Strategy for Healthcare Advancement through Knowledge, Technology and Innovation): Rs 10,000 Cr will be used to build the ecosystem for domestic production of biologics and biosimilars over the next 5 years. • A biopharma-centric national network will be developed by setting up three new NIPERs (National Institutes of Pharmaceutical Education and Research) and upgrading seven existing ones. • It will also create a network of over 1000 accredited India Clinical Trials sites. ii. India Semiconductor Mission (ISM): ISM 2.0 will be launched to produce equipment and materials, design full-stack Indian IP (Intellectual Property), and increase supply chains. iii. Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme: This was launched in April 2025 with an outlay of Rs 22,919 Cr to develop a robust component ecosystem by attracting large investments (global/domestic) in the electronics component manufacturing ecosystem. • In this Budget, it was proposed to increase the outlay to Rs 40,000 Cr. iv. Earth Corridors: This year’s budget is proposed to support the mineral-rich States of Odisha, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh (AP) and Tamil Nadu (TN) to establish dedicated Rare Earth Corridors to promote mining, processing, research and manufacturing. v. Chemical Parks: Government to launch a Scheme to support States in establishing 3 dedicated Chemical Parks to enhance domestic chemical production and reduce import dependency. vi. Integrated Programme for the Textile Sector announced: This programme has following 5 sub parts: • The National Fibre Scheme for self-reliance in natural fibres such as silk, wool and jute, man- made fibres, and new-age fibres. • Textile Expansion and Employment Scheme to modernize traditional clusters with capital support for machinery, technology upgradation and common testing and certification centres.

Rejuvenating legacy industrial sectors: The scheme proposes to revive 200 legacy industrial clusters to improve their cost competitiveness and efficiency through infrastructure and technology upgradation. Creating “Champion Small and Medium Enterprise (SME)”: The budget has proposed a three pronged approach to help SMEs grow as ‘Champions’. • A dedicated Rs 10,000 Cr SME Growth Fund, to be introduced, to create future Champions, incentivizing enterprises based on select criteria. • Self-Reliant India (SRI) Fund to be allocated with additional Rs 2,000 Cr, to continue support to micro enterprises and maintain their access to risk capital. • Government to facilitate Professional Institutions such as ICAI (Institute of Chartered Accountants of India), ICSI (Institute of Company Secretaries of India), ICMAI (Institute of Cost Accountants of India) to design short-term, modular courses and practical tools to develop a cadre of ‘Corporate Mitras’. Ease of Doing Business Individual Persons Resident Outside India (PROI) will be permitted to invest in equity instruments of listed Indian companies through the Portfolio Investment Scheme. • It is also proposed to increase the investment limit for an individual PROI under this scheme from 5% to 10%, with an overall investment limit for all individual PROIs to 24%, from the current 10%. 2. Second Kartavya – Fulfil aspirations and build capacity High-Powered ‘Education to Employment and Enterprise’ Standing Committee: The committee will be set up to recommend measures that focus on the service sector. Creation of Professionals: Existing institutions for Allied Health Professionals (AHPs) to be upgraded and 10,000 new AHP Institutions to be established in private and Government sectors. • 5 Regional Medical Hubs to be established, to promote India as a hub for medical tourism services. Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, and Homeopathy (AYUSH): 3 new All India Institutes of Ayurveda to be established. • Upgrade AYUSH pharmacies and Drug Testing Labs for higher standards of certification ecosystem. • Upgrade the World Health Organisation (WHO) Global Traditional Medicine Centre (GTMC) in Jamnagar (Gujarat) to bolster evidence-based research, training and awareness for traditional medicine. Animal Husbandry: To scale up availability of veterinary professionals by more than 20,000, it is proposed to roll out a loan-linked capital subsidy support scheme for establishment of veterinary and paravet colleges, veterinary hospitals, diagnostic laboratories and breeding facilities. Orange Economy: The Government proposed to support the Indian Institute of Creative Technologies, Mumbai, in setting up AVGC (Animation, Visual Effects, Gaming and Comics) Content Creator Labs in 15,000 schools and 500 colleges. • India’s Animation, Visual Effects, Gaming and Comics (AVGC) sector is a growing industry, projected to require 2 million professionals by 2030. Education: Five University Townships will be developed near major industrial and logistics corridors through the challenge route, along with the establishment of one girls’ hostel in every district through Viability Gap Fund (VGF)/capital support.

Tourism: National Council for Hotel Management and Catering Technology to be upgraded to National Institute of Hospitality. • A pilot scheme for upskilling 10,000 guides in 20 tourist sites was announced through a standardized, high-quality 12-week training course in hybrid mode in collaboration with an Indian Institute of Management (IIM). • A National Destination Digital Knowledge Grid to be established to digitally document all places of significance. Heritage and Sports: 15 archeological sites including Lothal (Gujarat), Dholavira (Gujarat), Rakhigarhi (Haryana), Adichanallur (TN), Sarnath (UP), Hastinapur (UP), and Leh Palace (Ladakh) to be developed into vibrant, experiential cultural destinations. • Khelo India Mission to be launched to transform the Sports sector over the next decade. 3. Third Kartavya This is aligned with vision of Sabka Sath, Sabka Vikas and requires targeted efforts in the following four areas: Increasing Farmer Incomes: New Initiatives to be undertaken for Integrated development of 500 reservoirs and Amrit Sarovars. • High Value Agriculture: Coconut Promotion Scheme to be launched to increase production and enhance productivity. • A dedicated programme is proposed for Indian cashew and cocoa to make India self-reliant in raw cashew and cocoa production and processing • Government to launch Bharat-VISTAAR (Virtually Integrated System to Access Agricultural Resources), a multilingual Artificial Intelligence (AI) tool to integrate the AgriStack portals and the ICAR (Indian Council of Agricultural Research) package on agricultural practices with AI systems. Empowering Divyangjan: The Divyangjan Kaushal Yojana is proposed to provide task-oriented and process-driven employment opportunities for Divyangjans in the IT, AVGC, hospitality, and food and beverage sectors. Commitment to Mental Health and Trauma Care: Government to set up NIMHANS-2 (National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences) in north India and also upgrade National Mental Health Institutes in Ranchi (Jharkhand) and Tezpur (Assam) as Regional Apex Institutions. Focus on the Purvodaya States: Development of an integrated East Coast Industrial Corridor with a well-connected node at Durgapur (WB), creation of 5 tourism destinations in the 5 Purvodaya States, and the provision of 4,000 e-buses. • Buddhist Circuits: A scheme to be launched for the development of Buddhist Circuits in Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Assam, Manipur, Mizoram and Tripura. 16th Finance Commission (FC): The Report of the 16th FC (Chair: Dr. Arvind Panagariya) was submitted in the Parliament on February 1, 2026. • The 16th FC has recommended that the Central Government retain the 41% share of tax devolution to the States that had been implemented since 2021. • The recommendations will apply for the five-year period between 2026-27 and 2030-31.

Criteria for Devolution PART B Direct Tax New Income Tax (IT) Act: The New IT Act ,2025 to come into effect from April 2026. Ease of Living: Interest awarded by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal to a natural person will be exempt from IT. • Single window filing with depositories for Form 15G or 15 H for TDS on dividends, interests etc. • Extend time available for revising returns from 31st December to 31st March with payment of nominal fees. • An automated scheme for small taxpayers to obtain lower or nil deduction certificates. Tax Collection at Source (TCS): Reduce TCS rate on sale of overseas tour program package to 2%. • Reduce the TCS rate to 2% (from current 5%) for Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) remittances for education and medical. • Supply of manpower services will be explicitly covered under TDS provisions for payments to contractors, with TDS applicable at 1% or 2% to remove ambiguity. • TCS rate for sellers of specific goods namely alcoholic liquor, scrap and minerals will be rationalized to 2% and that on tendu leaves will be reduced from 5% to 2%. Foreign Asset Disclosure Scheme: This scheme would be applicable for two categories of taxpayers namely, • (A) who did not disclose their overseas income or asset and (B) who disclosed their overseas income and/or paid due tax, but could not declare the asset acquired. • For category (A), the limit of undisclosed income/asset is proposed to be up to 1 Cr rupees. • For category (B), asset value is proposed to be up to 5 Cr rupees. Here, immunity from both penalty and prosecution will be available with the payment of fee of 1 lakh rupees. Rationalizing Penalty and Prosecution: No interest will be charged on penalty amounts during the appeal period before the first appellate authority, while the pre-payment requirement will be reduced from 20% to 10% of the core tax demand.

# Page 14^page=14
Report Errors in the PDF - support@affairscloud.com Copyright 2014-2026 @ AffairsCloud.com 14 Union Budget 2026-27 • Taxpayers will be permitted to update returns even after reassessment proceedings have commenced, subject to an additional 10% tax, to reduce litigation. • The existing immunity framework for underreporting will be extended to cases of misreporting, subject to payment of an additional 100% of the tax amount over and above the applicable tax and interest. • Non-disclosure of non-immovable foreign assets valued below Rs 20 lakh will be granted immunity from prosecution with retrospective effect from 1 October 2024. Cooperatives: Dividend income received by a notified national cooperative federation from investments made up to 31 January 2026 will be exempt for three years, provided the dividends are distributed to member co-operatives. Supporting IT sector: The threshold for availing safe harbour for IT services to be enhanced from Rs 300 Cr to Rs 2,000 Cr. • Safe harbour for IT services shall be approved by an automated rule-driven process, and can be continued for a period of 5 years at a stretch. • Unilateral Advanced Pricing Agreement (APA) process for IT services to be fast-tracked with the endeavour to conclude it within a period of 2 years, which can be extended by 6 months on taxpayer’s request. Attracting global investments: A safe harbour of 15% on cost to be provided if the company providing data centre services from India is a related entity. • Exemption from income tax for 5 years to be provided to any non-resident who provides capital goods, equipment or tooling. • Exemption to global (non-India sourced) income of a non-resident expert, for a stay period of 5 years under notified schemes. • Exemption from Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) to all non-residents who pay tax on presumptive basis. Other Tax Proposals: Buybacks will be taxed as capital gains for all shareholders, with promoters liable to an additional buyback tax, resulting in an effective tax of 22% for corporate and 30% for non-corporate promoters. • Securitisation Transaction Tax (STT): STT on Futures to be raised to 0.05% from present 0.02%. o STT on options premium and exercise of options to be raised to 0.15% from the present rate of 0.1% and 0.125% respectively. Indirect Tax Marine, leather, and textile products: The limit for duty-free imports of specified inputs used for processing seafood products for export, to increase from the current 1% to 3% of the FOB (Free On Board) value. Energy Transition: The basic customs duty exemption given to capital goods used for manufacturing Lithium-Ion Cells for batteries to be extended. • The basic customs duty on import of sodium antimonate for use in manufacture of solar glass to be exempted. Nuclear Power: The existing basic customs duty exemption on imports of goods required for Nuclear Power Projects to be extended till the year 2035.

Report Errors in the PDF - support@affairscloud.com Copyright 2014-2026 @ AffairsCloud.com 15 Union Budget 2026-27 Critical Minerals: The basic customs duty to the import of capital goods required for processing of critical minerals to be exempted. Biogas blended CNG (Compressed Natural Gas): The entire value of biogas while calculating the Central Excise duty payable on biogas blended CNG to be excluded. Civil and Defence Aviation: The basic customs duty on components and parts required for the manufacture of civilian, training and other aircrafts to be exempted. • The basic custom duty on raw materials imported for manufacture of parts of aircraft to be used in maintenance, repair, or overhaul requirements by Units in the Defence sector to be exempted. Electronics: The basic customs duty on specified parts used in the manufacture of microwave ovens to be exempted. Special Economic Zone (SEZ): A one-time measure is proposed to allow eligible SEZ manufacturing units to sell in the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) at concessional duty rates. Ease of Living: The tariff rate on all dutiable goods imported for personal use to be reduced from 20% to 10%. • The basic customs duty on 17 drugs/ medicines is to be exempted. • Duty free personal import of drugs/ medicines and food for 7 more rare diseases. Trust-based systems: Duty deferral period for Tier 2 and Tier 3 Authorised Economic Operators, known as AEOs, to be enhanced from 15 days to 30 days. • Validity period of advance ruling, binding on Customs, to be extended from the present 3 years to 5 years. New export opportunities: The removal of the Rs 10 lakh per consignment cap on courier exports will enable small businesses, artisans, and start-ups to access global e-commerce markets. Annual Financial Statement (AFS): The AFS, as mandated under Article 112, shows the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India for 2026-27, along with estimates for 2025-26 and actuals for the year 2024-25. • The receipts and disbursements are shown under three parts in which Government Accounts are kept viz., The Consolidated Fund of India (CFI), The Contingency Fund of India and The Public Account of India. 2. Demands for Grants (DG): DG are the documents through which the government places before the Lok Sabha its estimated requirements for expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India for a financial year. • Each DG sets out the amount of funds a ministry or department seeks to spend during the year. 3. Finance Bill: Along with the AFS, a Finance Bill is presented before Parliament under Article 110(1)(a) of the Constitution to provide for tax-related proposals in the Budget. 4. Fiscal Policy Statements mandated under Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003: • Macro-Economic Framework Statement: This contains an assessment of the growth prospects of the economy along with the statement of underlying assumptions. • Medium-Term Fiscal Policy cum Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement: It sets out the three year rolling targets for specific fiscal indicators in relation to GDP at market prices, namely FD; RD; PD; Tax Revenue; Non-tax Revenue and Central Government Debt.
